polygon-apothem.context: A regular hexagon with a dot at its centre and a short line running from the centre to the middle of one side, meeting it at a right angle. Used for polygon area formulas and geometry lessons.

polygon-diagonals.context: A hexagon with three lines fanning from one top corner to the other far corners, splitting it into triangles. Used to show diagonals, triangulation and interior angle sums.

osculating-circle.context: A curve bending like a bowl with a circle sitting snugly in its bend, and a short radius line from the circle centre down to the point where they touch. Used in calculus and curvature lessons.

squaring-the-circle.context: A circle and a square drawn over each other on the same centre, with the same area. Stands for the classic problem of constructing a square equal in area to a given circle.

apollonian-gasket.context: A large circle packed with three touching circles and smaller circles filling the gaps between them. Used for circle packing, fractals and tangent circle problems.

nested-squares.context: A square with a tilted square inside whose corners touch the midpoints of the sides, and another square inside that. Used for recursion, inscribed shapes and pattern design.

curve-stitching.context: Two lines meeting at a right angle with straight threads joining points on one line to points on the other, so the threads trace a smooth curve. Used for string art and envelope curves.

geometric-translation.context: A triangle and an identical copy shifted up and to the right, with a straight arrow joining one corner to the matching corner. Shows a translation, a slide without turning.

geometric-dilation.context: A small triangle and a larger copy inside and around a centre dot, with lines running from the centre through matching corners. Shows a dilation or enlargement about a point.

glide-reflection.context: Flag shaped triangles stepping along a dashed line, each one flipped to the opposite side of the line from the last. Shows a glide reflection, a slide combined with a mirror flip.

limacon.context: A looping closed curve with a smaller loop inside a larger one, both meeting at one point marked with a dot. Used for polar graphs and plane curves.

involute-curve.context: A circle with a taut line unwinding from it, and a curve traced by the free end of the line spreading outward. Used for gear teeth, evolutes and cord unwinding problems.

cubic-curve.context: An S shaped curve rising through the crossing of two axes, flattening briefly at the middle. Stands for a cubic function such as y equals x cubed.

absolute-value-graph.context: A sharp V shaped line sitting on crossed axes with its point at the origin. Stands for the graph of absolute value, the modulus function.

tangent-graph.context: Steep repeating curves crossing a horizontal axis between dashed vertical asymptote lines. Stands for the graph of the tangent function in trigonometry.

euler-spiral.context: An S shaped curve with an almost straight middle that coils tighter into a small spiral at each end. Used for road and railway transition curves and in physics.

fermat-spiral.context: Two spiral arms winding out from one shared centre, each lying between the turns of the other. Used for polar curves and the seed patterns of flower heads.

square-spiral.context: A spiral made of straight lines turning at right angles, growing longer with every turn. Used for mazes, number spirals and labyrinth designs.

spiral-of-theodorus.context: Right triangles joined around one shared point, each slightly larger than the last, curling like a snail shell. Shows how square roots are built from a chain of right triangles.

phyllotaxis-spiral.context: Round dots set in crossing spiral arms around a centre, like the seed head of a sunflower. Used for golden angle patterns and plant growth.

tractrix.context: A curve falling from a vertical line and sweeping outward to approach a horizontal line, with a short tangent segment ending on the horizontal line. Used for pursuit curves and the shape of a pseudosphere.

nephroid.context: A kidney shaped closed curve pinched inward on each side into two points. Used for caustics and plane curves made by rolling circles.

epicycloid.context: A flower shaped curve with five sharp points, traced by a small circle rolling around the outside of a larger one. Used for gear profiles and spirograph style patterns.

cassini-oval.context: A peanut shaped closed curve pinched in the middle, with a dot at the heart of each lobe marking the two foci. Used for curves defined by a product of distances.

full-angle.context: A single ray from a centre dot with a circular arrow sweeping all the way round it. Marks a full angle of 360 degrees, one complete turn.

penrose-tiling.context: A five pointed star made of kite and dart shaped tiles fitting together around its centre. Used for aperiodic tilings, quasicrystals and decorative floors.

rhombille-tiling.context: A stack of hexagons each split into three rhombuses, so the pattern looks like a field of tumbling cubes. Used for tiling patterns and optical illusion designs.

octagon-square-tiling.context: Four octagons meeting with a small square filling the gap between them. Used for bathroom floors, paving and truncated square tilings.

trihexagonal-tiling.context: Hexagons separated by small triangles so the joining lines form a star of lines pattern like a woven lattice. Used for kagome patterns and basket weave designs.

truchet-tiles.context: A square filled with quarter circle arcs in the corners, joined into winding curves. Used for generative art and maze like patterns built from repeated tiles.

islamic-geometric-pattern.context: An eight pointed star at the centre of a square, with straight bands forming a lattice around it. Used for tile work, mosaics and star and polygon ornament.

fish-scale-pattern.context: Rows of overlapping semicircle scallops stacked in offset layers, like fish scales or roof shingles. Used for scale, wave and seigaiha style patterns.

basketweave-pattern.context: Pairs of parallel bars alternating between horizontal and vertical in a checkerboard layout. Used for woven textures, parquet floors and brick paving.

pentomino.context: Five equal squares joined edge to edge into an irregular block shape. Used for tiling puzzles and polyomino packing problems.

hexaflexagon.context: A flat paper hexagon folded from a strip, divided into six triangles with every other one shaded. Used for paper folding toys and recreational maths.

dragon-curve.context: A single line of short right angle turns that folds into a curled dragon shaped outline. Used for fractals and paper folding sequences.

cantor-set.context: Stacked horizontal bars where each row splits the bar above into two by removing its middle third. Used to explain the Cantor set, fractals and infinity.

menger-sponge.context: A cube seen from a corner with a square hole through the centre of each face and smaller holes around it. Used for fractals and volume and surface area paradoxes.

pythagoras-tree.context: A fractal tree built from squares, each topped with a right triangle that carries two smaller squares. Used for the Pythagorean theorem and fractal plant shapes.

sierpinski-carpet.context: A square with its middle ninth removed, and each of the remaining squares having its own middle removed in turn. Used for fractals and self similar patterns.

h-tree-fractal.context: An H shape with a smaller H at each of its four tips, repeated two levels deep. Used for fractals and clock distribution layouts in chip design.

borromean-rings.context: Three circles linked in a triangle arrangement, each passing over one ring and under the other, so no two are linked alone. Used for knots, links and symbols of unity.

hopf-link.context: Two circles interlocked like a pair of chain links, each passing through the other. Used for topology, knot theory and link symbols.

triskelion.context: Three curved spiral arms radiating from a shared centre, each ending in a small coil. Used for Celtic art, heraldry and symbols of threefold motion.

kanizsa-triangle.context: Three discs with wedges cut out, arranged so the gaps suggest a bright triangle that is not actually drawn. Used for illusory contours and vision science.

muller-lyer-illusion.context: Two equal horizontal lines, one capped with inward pointing arrowheads and one with outward pointing fins, so they look different in length. Used for optical illusion examples.

ebbinghaus-illusion.context: Two equal centre circles, one ringed by big circles and one ringed by small circles, so they look different in size. Used for size perception demos.

cafe-wall-illusion.context: Rows of dark and light bricks shifted against each other so the straight lines between rows look tilted. Used for optical illusion examples and pattern design.

hering-illusion.context: Two straight parallel lines crossing a fan of lines that radiate from a centre, so the straight lines seem to bow outward. Used for optical illusion examples.

spherical-coordinates.context: A sphere with a point on its surface, a radius line from the centre to it, and arcs marking the angle from the vertical axis and around the horizontal plane. Used for radius, polar and azimuth angles.

orthographic-views.context: Front, top and side outlines of one simple block arranged in an L layout. Used for engineering drawings and technical drawing lessons.

delaunay-triangulation.context: Scattered points joined by straight lines into a mesh of irregular triangles. Used in computational geometry, terrain models and mesh generation.

convex-hull.context: Scattered points wrapped by an outer polygon pulled tight around them like a rubber band. Used in computational geometry, collision detection and data analysis.

riemann-sum.context: A rising curve on axes with a row of rectangles beneath it whose tops touch the curve. Used to show how integrals are approximated by adding up rectangle areas.

area-under-curve.context: A curve on crossed axes with the region between the curve and the horizontal axis filled in. Stands for a definite integral as the area under a graph.

function-mapping-diagram.context: Two tall ovals holding dots, with arrows running from dots in the left oval to dots in the right oval. Used to show a function mapping inputs to outputs.

sphere-in-cylinder.context: A sphere fitting snugly inside a cylinder, touching its top, bottom and curved side. Used for Archimedes volume ratios and solid geometry.

rhombitrihexagonal-tiling.context: A central hexagon ringed by alternating squares and small triangles, part of a repeating tiling. Used for semiregular tilings and ornamental floors.

pythagorean-tiling.context: Large squares and small squares interlocking in an offset pinwheel pattern, like hopscotch paving. Used to illustrate the Pythagorean theorem with two square sizes.

vicsek-fractal.context: A plus shaped cross of five squares where each square is itself a smaller cross of five squares. Used for self similar fractals and cross shaped patterns.

euler-diagram.context: A large circle holding a smaller circle inside it, with a third circle standing apart and a dot inside the large circle. Shows subsets and separate sets in logic and set theory.

triple-venn-diagram.context: Three overlapping circles arranged in a triangle, with the region shared by all three filled in. Used for comparing three groups and showing their common overlap.

triangular-numbers.context: Dots stacked into growing triangles with one dot, then three, then six. Used to show triangular numbers and number patterns.

polyiamond.context: Four equal triangles joined edge to edge into a slanted strip that zigzags along its length. Used for triangle tiling puzzles and polyform mathematics.

lattice-polygon.context: A polygon drawn on a square grid of dots, with every corner sitting exactly on a dot. Used for Pick's theorem and area by counting grid points.

faces-edges-vertices.context: A cube with its top face shaded, its three visible edges from one corner drawn and another corner marked with a dot. Used to teach faces, edges and vertices of solid shapes.

conical-spiral.context: A cone with a spiral stripe winding up its side from the wide base toward the point. Used for helices on cones, spiral springs and 3D curves.

aperiodic-monotile.context: A single thirteen sided tile known as the hat, outlined on its own. Stands for the shape that can cover a plane forever without the pattern ever repeating.

cairo-pentagonal-tiling.context: Irregular house shaped pentagons fitted together at right angles, like the paving of a Cairo street. Used for tessellation patterns and floor design.

spherical-shell.context: A ring with one quarter cut away and a hollow centre, standing for a hollow sphere with a wedge removed so the thin wall and empty inside show. Used for shells, volume and cross sections.

ponzo-illusion.context: Two rail lines leaning toward each other at the top, with two equal short bars between them at different heights. Used as an example of perspective and size illusions.

poggendorff-illusion.context: A vertical bar with a diagonal line entering from one side and leaving from the other, the two halves looking out of line. Used as an example of misalignment illusions.

jastrow-illusion.context: Two identical curved bands stacked one above the other, with the lower one looking larger than the upper. Used as an example of size illusions.

hermann-grid-illusion.context: A three by three grid of black squares separated by white lines, where grey dots seem to appear at the white crossings. Used as an example of vision and contrast illusions.

four-color-map.context: A square map divided into four irregular regions, each marked differently so no two neighbours match. Stands for the four colour theorem and map colouring.

kolam-pattern.context: A rounded four lobed shape wrapped around a diamond of five dots. Stands for kolam, the dot grid floor drawings made in South India.

asanoha-pattern.context: A six pointed star with thin triangular cuts radiating from its centre. Stands for asanoha, the hemp leaf pattern used in Japanese textiles and woodwork.
